lessons.title: Users and groups: /etc/passwd and /etc/group
lessons.goal:
Learn where Linux stores accounts, what each field means, and how the kernel uses numbers (UID and GID), not names.

Why it matters: ownership, permissions and "who is running this" questions all come down to these files and numbers.

setup.note: Steps that create a test user use sudo. Run them on a throwaway machine. The user `demo1` is removed at the end.

steps.title: Who am I?
steps.text: `id` shows your UID, primary group and all groups. The kernel only knows these **numbers**. Names are a convenience added by libraries.

steps.title: One line per user in /etc/passwd
steps.text: Seven fields separated by colons: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The `x` means the password hash is in `/etc/shadow`. `getent` reads the account databases the way programs do.

steps.title: Groups in /etc/group
steps.text: Format `name:x:GID:members`. The **primary group** comes from the GID field in passwd. **Supplementary groups** are listed here.

steps.title: UID ranges and UID 0
steps.text: UID **0** is root. The kernel gives it special power (capabilities), whatever the name. System accounts use low numbers, normal users start at `UID_MIN`.

steps.title: Create a user
steps.text: `useradd` adds a line to `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` (and `/etc/shadow`), and `-m` creates the home directory.

steps.title: Files store numbers
steps.text: `ls -n` shows the raw owner numbers. If the name is deleted from passwd, the file keeps its number.

run.cmd: touch mine; sudo chown demo1 mine; ls -l mine | awk '{print $3}'
sudo userdel -r demo1; ls -ln mine | awk '{print $3}'; ls -l mine | awk '{print $3}'

steps.under: The inode stores a 32-bit owner number. When `ls` prints a name, the C library calls `getpwuid()`, which reads the sources listed in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (files, then maybe LDAP or SSSD). After the user is deleted the lookup fails and `ls` falls back to the number. A new user created later with the same UID would silently own the file.

quiz.q: What does the kernel use to identify the owner of a file?
quiz.explain: Names exist only in user space.

quiz.q: Which field of /etc/passwd holds the login shell?
quiz.explain: name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. The shell is the seventh.

quiz.q: What happens to a deleted user's files?
quiz.explain: Step 6: `ls -l` shows the number after the user is removed.

quiz.q: Which command reads accounts the way programs do (through NSS)?
quiz.explain: `getent` follows nsswitch.conf, so it also finds LDAP/SSSD users.

check.scenario: You find files owned by UID 1234 on a disk from another server, and no such user exists here. What are the risks of simply creating a user with UID 1234?
check.answer: The new user instantly owns all those files and can read or change them. Check what the files are first. Prefer `chown` to the correct local user, or map IDs deliberately.

lessons.title: Passwords, su and sudo
lessons.goal:
Learn where password hashes live, how `su` and `sudo` differ, and how to give a user exactly one privileged command.

Why it matters: sudo configuration is one of the most security-relevant files on a server, and a syntax error in it can lock you out.

setup.note: Steps that create a test user use sudo. Run them on a throwaway machine. The user `demo1` is removed at the end.

steps.title: /etc/shadow is locked down
steps.text: Password hashes are not in `/etc/passwd`, which everyone can read. They are in `/etc/shadow`, which ordinary users cannot read.

run.cmd: sudo useradd -m demo1 && echo 'demo1:Test-pass-123' | sudo chpasswd

steps.after: We print only the first three characters of the hash field. `$6$` means SHA-512 on this system (newer distributions use `$y$`, yescrypt). The last field is the maximum password age in days.

steps.title: Locking an account
steps.text: `passwd -l` puts `!!` in front of the hash. The password can no longer match. `-u` removes it.

run.output:
Locking password for user demo1.
passwd: Success

Unlocking password for user demo1.
passwd: Success

steps.title: su starts a shell as another user
steps.text: `su - USER` (with the dash) starts a **login shell**: it sets HOME, PATH and the working directory as for a new login. Without the dash you keep most of your old environment. Root can use `su` without a password.

steps.title: sudo runs one command with another identity
steps.text: `sudo` is a setuid-root program. It reads `/etc/sudoers`, checks whether you may run the command, and then runs it as the target user (root by default).

steps.title: Allow exactly one command
steps.text: Put rules in a file under `/etc/sudoers.d/`. Always check the syntax with `visudo -cf` **before** relying on it: a broken sudoers file can lock you out of sudo.
steps.under: `sudo` matches the command by its **full path**, so `cat` was not allowed. Never allow commands that can start a shell or edit arbitrary files (`vi`, `less`, `find`, `tar`) in a sudo rule: they give full root.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Remove the rule and the user.

run.cmd: sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/demo1; sudo userdel -r demo1; getent passwd demo1; echo "exit code: $?"

quiz.q: What is the difference between `su demo1` and `su - demo1`?
options: The dash starts a login shell with the user's environment
quiz.explain: With `-` you get HOME, PATH and directory of a fresh login.

quiz.q: Why use `visudo -cf FILE` before relying on a sudoers file?
options: A syntax error can disable sudo for everyone
quiz.explain: A broken sudoers file makes sudo refuse to work.

quiz.q: A sudo rule allows `/usr/bin/less`. Why is that dangerous?
options: You can start a shell from inside less and have root
quiz.explain: Typing `!sh` in less runs a root shell.

check.scenario: A junior admin edited /etc/sudoers directly and made a typo. `sudo` now says `syntax error` and everyone is locked out. How do you recover, and how do you prevent it next time?
check.answer: Get a root shell by another way (console/rescue mode, `su -` with the root password, or a recovery boot), fix the file. Prevent: edit only with `visudo` (it validates before saving) and keep local rules in `/etc/sudoers.d/` files checked by `visudo -cf`.

interview.a: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The x means the hash is in /etc/shadow. See [the lesson](#/lesson/4/passwd-group-files).
UID 0. The kernel gives the process all capabilities. The name `root` is only a label in /etc/passwd.

`su` switches to another account and needs **that account's** password (not for root). `sudo` runs single commands with your own password and logs each one, according to sudoers rules. See [the lesson](#/lesson/4/shadow-su-sudo).
/etc/passwd must be world-readable (many programs map UIDs to names), so hashes there could be attacked offline by anyone. /etc/shadow is readable only by root.

interview.q: How do you safely edit sudoers?
interview.a: With `visudo` (validates and locks) or drop-in files in /etc/sudoers.d/ checked with `visudo -cf`.

interview.q: A user is deleted but files remain. What happens?
interview.a: The files keep the numeric UID. Listing shows the number. Reusing the UID would hand the files to a new user.

glossary.def: Numeric user ID. The kernel uses it for ownership and permission checks.
Name Service Switch: the libc mechanism (nsswitch.conf) that decides where names come from (files, DNS, SSSD).
Root-only file with password hashes and ageing information.
The configuration that says who may run which commands as whom with sudo.
The shell started for a new login session; `su -` starts one.
